name: mdk
why: GNU MIX development kit for Knuth's hypothetical 1960s machine, a delightful way to watch an imaginary computer execute.

brief.what_it_is: GNU MDK (MIX Development Kit) is an emulator toolkit for Donald Knuth's MIX, the imaginary computer from The Art of Computer Programming, and its assembly language MIXAL. It takes MIXAL source files, which mixasm compiles into binary files that the MIX virtual machines run. The toolkit has two VM front ends: mixvm, a command-line debugger built on readline, and gmixvm, a GTK+ graphical one. It also includes mixguile, a Guile interpreter with an embedded MIX VM that can be scripted in Scheme, plus Emacs integration (mixal-mode.el and mixvm.el). Version 1.3.1 is the current release.
brief.why_it_exists: The page presents MIX as a teaching tool: MIX is a simplified version of real CISC computers, and its assembly language closely resembles real ones, so it can be used to learn computer architecture and assembly programming.
brief.how_it_works: MDK emulates MIX's registers, memory cells, overflow toggle, comparison flags, I/O devices and binary instruction set. mixasm translates MIXAL source into binaries that the VMs execute. The VMs support breakpoints, conditional breakpoints, step execution, timing statistics, instruction tracing, and inspection or modification of registers, flags and memory at any step, with I/O simulated through standard output and the file system.

commands_seen.context: Gets the MDK development source tree from the Savannah git repository (master branch).
Same repository over HTTP, for users behind a firewall that blocks the git protocol.

brief.install_notes: The page lists the source tarball from GNU's FTP site (or a mirror) as the stable download. The user's manual ships in texinfo format and is converted to info files during installation. Packages also exist via apt-get on Debian GNU/Linux (MDK is part of Debian), Fink packages for the CLI and GUI, and a MacPorts port. The page gives no hardware, account, or runtime requirements beyond the platform note and the GTK+ dependency for gmixvm.
brief.standout: It is a faithful emulator of a textbook machine that has been used in computer science courses for decades. Its mixguile front end embeds a Scheme interpreter with a MIX VM, so the machine can be driven and extended from Scheme code.
brief.status: Maintained. The page advertises GNU MDK 1.3.1 with a September 2025 release, and the page itself was updated 2025/09/24. The source is kept in a Savannah git repository. I did not check commit history directly.
brief.caveats: The page says MDK runs on any GNU or FreeBSD system and links to a supported-platforms list that I did not open. gmixvm needs GTK+. Building from source is required for the tarball route. The page's Creative Commons NoDerivatives license covers the web page only; the software is described as free software, but the page does not name its software license.

MDK (MIX Development Kit) offers an emulation of MIX and MIXAL.

judge.reason: A runnable emulator for Knuth’s fictional MIX machine makes textbook architecture tangible, with MIXAL debugging and even Scheme scripting through an embedded VM.

entry.title: mdk
entry.tldr: An emulator, assembler and debugger for MIX, the imaginary computer from Knuth's The Art of Computer Programming, so you can step through its assembly.
entry.deeper_look:
MDK emulates MIX, the made-up machine Donald Knuth invented for The Art of Computer Programming, and MIXAL, its assembly language. `mixasm` turns MIXAL source into binaries, and the virtual machines run them. The emulated machine includes registers, memory cells, an overflow toggle, comparison flags, I/O devices and the binary instruction set.

There are two front ends for the VM. `mixvm` is a command-line debugger built on readline, and `gmixvm` is a GTK+ graphical one. Both support breakpoints, conditional breakpoints, step execution, timing statistics and instruction tracing. You can inspect or change registers, flags and memory at any step. I/O is simulated through standard output and the file system.

The fourth executable, `mixguile`, is a Guile interpreter with a MIX VM embedded in it, so the machine can be driven and scripted from Scheme. The kit also ships Emacs modes for editing MIXAL and running the VM.

The idea underneath is that a deliberately simplified machine is a good place to learn how real ones work. The project's own words: "The MIX computer is a simplified version of real CISC computers, and its assembly language closely resembles real ones." Since the book's programs are written for MIX, this lets you run them and watch the state change instruction by instruction.

try_this.what_happens: Lists the options of the command-line MIX debugger, the quickest way to see what the VM can do.
Shows how to assemble a MIXAL source file into a binary the VM can run.
Shows the options for the graphical MIX VM, which needs GTK+.

entry.whats_unique: It is a faithful emulator of a textbook machine, with a Scheme-scriptable VM (`mixguile`) alongside the debugger front ends.
entry.caveats: The brief gives no worked example commands, so you will need Knuth's book or the bundled manual to know what MIXAL to write.
